title: Zahra Joya: The Taliban will collapse without support
gist: Interview with exiled Afghan journalist Zahra Joya, who argues the Taliban regime is externally dependent and would collapse without foreign support — while noting China, Russia and Iran are willing to supply it and that Afghan-Pakistan border fighting is the regime's real vulnerability. She wants gender apartheid recognised as a crime against humanity and UK aid channelled conditionally through independent NGOs.

insights.claim: Zahra Joya's core claim is that the Taliban cannot sustain itself independently and would collapse soon if other countries withheld support, making external patronage the regime's binding constraint.
insights.so_what: Frames Afghan regime risk as a function of third-party sponsorship rather than internal legitimacy — watch patron behaviour, not Kabul, for regime-change signals.
insights.quote: If they don’t receive support from other countries, I’m sure they’ll collapse soon.
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: China, Russia and Iran are identified as willing providers of support to the Taliban administration, undercutting the leverage of western non-recognition.
insights.so_what: Western sanctions and non-recognition lose bite where a rival bloc backfills — the standard pattern now repeating across sanctioned states.
insights.locator: Though, she notes, China, Russia and Iran
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: Joya treats recent Afghanistan-Pakistan border fighting as a positive development and hopes it widens, implying she sees regional conflict rather than western pressure as the more plausible destabiliser of Taliban rule.
insights.so_what: Af-Pak border escalation is the tail risk to monitor for South Asian security and refugee flows, and is more likely than diplomatic pressure to move the situation.
insights.quote: The good part is that they have this tension with Pakistan,
insights.locator: “The good part is that they have this tension
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: The US withdrawal from Bagram air base on the night of 2nd July 2021 was so abrupt that the incoming Afghan commander, General Mir Asadullah Kohistani, only realised the Americans had gone when he saw the power was off at dawn.
insights.so_what: A durable case study in allied-withdrawal risk: handover failure, not battlefield defeat, is what triggered the collapse — relevant to any assessment of US security guarantees.
insights.locator: Bagram air base, built by the Soviets
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

themes.theme: Gender apartheid as a legal category

insights.claim: Joya's first ask of the UK government is to push for gender apartheid to be recognised as a crime against humanity, on the same legal footing as racial apartheid.
insights.so_what: A new codified international crime would create fresh legal exposure and sanctions hooks for states and firms engaging with Kabul.
insights.quote: support us to push this gender apartheid to be recognised as a crime against humanity
insights.locator: Joya wants the UK government, first
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: Her second ask is UK backing for the International Criminal Court cases against two Taliban leaders, moving accountability from rhetoric to individual criminal liability.
insights.so_what: Named-individual ICC action constrains travel, asset access and any future normalisation track for the named leadership.
insights.locator: And, second, to support the International Criminal Court
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: Britain does not recognise the Taliban as Afghanistan's legitimate government but 'engages pragmatically' for purposes such as aid delivery; Joya argues even that engagement should be conditional and routed through independent NGOs wherever possible.
insights.so_what: Aid-channel conditionality is the practical policy fight — it determines whether humanitarian flows entrench or bypass the regime.
insights.locator: And though UK policy is to not recognise
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: The scope of Taliban restrictions has widened past education into public speech: women are barred from university education and government jobs, female UN staff cannot enter their offices, and in 2024 women were banned from speaking in public.
insights.so_what: Restrictions now reach UN operations directly, which constrains multilateral programme delivery and raises the cost of any aid presence in Afghanistan.
insights.quote: So many things are banned for women,
insights.locator: Things in Afghanistan are “getting worse day by day,”
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: Posters appearing in Afghan cities before Kabul fell — a headscarfed woman marked with a red cross, a burqa-clad woman with a green tick — served as an advance public signal of the coming rule set.
insights.so_what: Regimes telegraph their programme before they hold power; visible symbolic enforcement is a leading indicator worth tracking ahead of formal takeover.
insights.quote: Only one form of womanhood was acceptable now,
insights.locator: They showed two women, one in a headscarf
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: Rukhshana Media is run entirely from Joya's London flat with seven on-the-ground reporters in Afghanistan whose identities are known only to her, are renamed every year, and who are kept unaware of each other for security.
insights.so_what: A working template for compartmentalised reporting under authoritarian rule — the operational model any information business faces in hostile jurisdictions.
insights.quote: for security reasons, they do not even know each other
insights.locator: Rukhshana Media is run from Joya’s London flat
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: In 2024 Rukhshana broke the story of a woman gang-raped in a Taliban jail whose attackers filmed the assault as a threat, never anticipating she would leak the footage to the press.
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that even a flat-run exile outlet can generate globally consequential evidence — atrocity documentation is no longer gatekept by large institutions.
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: Joya reads Afghan women's position as part of a global trend, citing a Taliban official mocking Kamala Harris's 2024 defeat on X with the line that Americans were not ready to hand their nation to a woman.
insights.so_what: Authoritarian actors explicitly read western electoral outcomes as licence — a reminder that domestic political results carry direct international signalling effects.
insights.quote: Americans are not ready to hand over the reins of their great nation to a woman.
insights.locator: For Joya, what is happening to Afghan women
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: Joya survived the first Taliban era as a 'bacha posh' — living as a boy until puberty — which allowed her to attend school when other girls could not, showing that even total bans are evaded at the margin.
insights.so_what: Informal workarounds mean prohibition data understates actual participation — a caution when reading any authoritarian regime's compliance statistics.
insights.locator: She was four when the Taliban first took over
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber

insights.claim: The human cost of exile is presented as ongoing rather than resolved: Joya cannot return, two siblings remain abroad unable to immigrate to the UK, and she describes exile as being safe while your soul burns.
insights.so_what: Family-reunification bottlenecks keep diaspora advocates permanently engaged with host-state policy — a persistent political constituency in the UK.
insights.quote: Sometimes exile is just that, being in a safe country while your soul burns.
insights.locator: In the memoir, she puts it like this
insights.speaker: Alona Ferber
